newsitem.title: INDIA: Mother Teresa given mild shock to regulate heart.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa given mild shock to regulate heart.

text.p: Doctors gave Mother Teresa a mild electric shock on Monday for the second time in six days to correct her faltering heart.
Doctors treating the 86-year-old nun at Calcutta's B.M. Birla Heart Research Centre said in a regular medical update that they performed the procedure in the afternoon.
"This was successful and tolerated well," the update said.
"Doctors hope that she remains in regular rhythm since this is best for Mother's condition and prognosis."
Doctors stabilised the Roman Catholic missionary's heartbeat with a mild electric shock last Wednesday but it began faltering again late on Sunday. They decided to repeat the procedure on Monday.
Mother Teresa was sedated and a shock pad attached to her chest, the doctors said. The mild electric current was then applied.
"Her condition is stabilising," they said shortly after the procedure was completed. "This afternoon she sat on a chair and had a late lunch since she was kept fasting all morning."

Mother Teresa was in hospital recovering from heart surgery last month, the third operation in five years to clear blocked coronary arteries. Her recovery has been complicated by her irregular heartbeat as well as lung and kidney problems.
Dogged by bronchitis from her youth, the charismatic nun's recovery continues to be slowed by her bronchial troubles.
"Her pulmonary condition still continues to be a problem but it is more under control," the bulletin said.
Dr Tarun Praharaj, a member of the panel treating Mother Teresa, said: "She is still having bronchial infection which is delaying her recovery. We are still observing her condition."
He warned that Mother Teresa, fitted with a heart pacemaker in 1989, was not yet out of danger. Her heart might once again lapse into its erratic rhythm.
"She is still not out of danger," Praharaj said. "The previous lung problem and the bronchial pneumonia are creating the problems. We cannot say this would not happen again."
The 1979 Nobel Peace Prize winner is revered for her work with the sick, the poor and the dying, for which she has been dubbed "Saint of the Gutters".
She is impatient to resume her work as the head of her Missionaries of Charity religious order, and has been imploring doctors to let her go home.
"She is only saying that she has to go back home since there is so much work to do for the poor people," Praharaj said.
Doctors hope she will be well enough to go home for Christmas, but they have warned that her recovery will be slow and that she might never be as active as before.
